Linearized polynomial maps
over finite fields

Joost Berson
Abstract

We consider polynomial maps described by so-called (multivariate) linearized polynomials. These polynomials are defined using a fixed prime power, say qq. Linearized polynomials have no mixed terms. Considering invertible polynomial maps without mixed terms over a characteristic zero field, we will only obtain (up to a linear transformation of the variables) triangular maps, which are the most basic examples of polynomial automorphisms. However, over the finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} automorphisms defined by linearized polynomials have (in general) an entirely different structure. Namely, we will show that the linearized polynomial maps over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} are in one-to-one correspondence with matrices having coefficients in a univariate polynomial ring over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Furthermore, composition of polynomial maps translates to matrix multiplication, implying that invertible linearized polynomial maps correspond to invertible matrices.

This alternate description of the linearized polynomial automorphism subgroup leads to the solution of many famous conjectures (most notably, the Jacobian Conjecture) for this kind of polynomials and polynomial maps.

Keywords: Affine space; polynomials over commutative rings; group of polynomial automorphisms; group of tame automorphisms

1 Introduction

Let K⁡[X]:=K⁡[X1,…,Xn]K[X]:=K[X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{n}] be a polynomial ring over a field KK. A natural problem in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry is to understand the group GAn⁡(K)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(K) of automorphisms of K⁡[X]K[X] preserving KK. There are various long-standing open problems and conjectures in affine algebraic geometry concerning polynomial rings and their automorphisms (see [10], [11] and [15] for more details). Below we mention a few of the most famous ones. (Precise definitions will be provided in later sections.)

Polynomial automorphisms are generally studied over a field of characteristic zero, but the prime characteristic case is gaining interest (for example in [2],[6],[8],[19] and [22]). In Section 4 of this paper, for the problems and conjectures mentioned below, we give a complete answer in cases involving linearized polynomials (over a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}), the main objects of interest of this paper. These polynomials, which are by definition (Section 3) 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear combinations of monomials of the form XiqmX_{i}^{{}^{q^{m}}}, have thus far only been studied in case n=1n=1, first by Ore in [23] and [24] (more on that in the same section). Section 3 is also devoted to a proof of the fact that the linearized polynomial maps over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} are in one-to-one correspondence with matrices having coefficients in a univariate polynomial ring over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} (where 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} is the finite field with qq elements).

Finally, in Section 5, we will emphasize the exceptional nature of linearized polynomial maps over finite fields. Namely, these maps form a special example of polynomial maps without mixed terms, which can be studied over a field of any characteristic. But the main result of this last section is that, over a characteristic zero field, every automorphism defined by polynomials without mixed terms is a triangular automorphism (after a linear transformation of the variables). This is certainly not the case for linearized polynomial maps over a finite field. Also, the other problems and conjectures mentioned below are discussed for the case of polynomials without mixed terms.

Tame Generators Problem: Give necessary and sufficient conditions for tameness of automorphisms of K⁡[X]K[X].

In two variables, this has already been solved by Jung [13] and Van der Kulk [16], saying that all automorphisms in two variables are tame. In more variables there is only one big result: Shestakov and Umirbaev gave a criterion for tameness (over characteristic zero fields) of automorphisms of the form (f1​(X1,X2,X3),f2​(X1,X2,X3),X3)(f_{1}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}),f_{2}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}),X_{3}) in their groundbreaking paper [25]. This gave a negative answer to the question of tameness of the famous Nagata automorphism, introduced in [21] (viewed as an automorphism in three variables over a field). We will show that all linearized polynomial automorphisms are tame, in any dimension (Theorem 4.2).

Jacobian Conjecture: If a polynomial map ff over a field KK with char⁡(K)=0\operatorname{char}(K)=0 has invertible Jacobian matrix, then ff itself is invertible.

This famous conjecture was first proposed by Keller [14] in 1939 for K=ℂK=\mathbb{C}. After more than six decades of intensive study by mathematicians, the conjecture is still open, even for the case n = 2. It is listed as one of the 18 important mathematical problems for the 21st century in Smale’s list [26]. More background and (references to) partial results on the Jacobian Conjecture can be found in [4] and [10]. In nonzero characteristic the conjecture is easily shown to be false, but we will present an analogue of this conjecture for linearized polynomial maps, and give a proof (Corollary 4.3).

Coordinate Recognition Problem: Given a polynomial f∈K⁡[X]f\in K[X], give necessary and sufficient conditions for ff to be a coordinate.

In case we have two variables, this problem has already been solved in [7] and in [9]. The Coordinate Recognition Problem is still open for three or more variables. Our Proposition 4.4 describes exactly when a linearized polynomial is a coordinate.

Polynomial Ring Recognition Problem: For a finitely generated KK-algebra AA, give necessary and sufficient conditions for AA to be (isomorphic to) a polynomial ring over KK.

A necessary condition for being a polynomial ring over KK is that AA is a domain. Surprisingly, if AA is defined by linearized polynomials this is also sufficient (Corollary 4.10). This doesn’t hold in general for an algebra defined over a field of characteristic zero, where the problem has only been solved in case AA is at most two-generated over KK. Corollary 4.10 also implies the Abhyankar-Sathaye Conjecture below, but then for linearized polynomials over a finite field (Theorem 4.11). In characteristic zero, this conjecture has only been completely solved for n≤2n\leq 2.

Abhyankar-Sathaye Conjecture: If char⁡(K)=0\operatorname{char}(K)=0 and f∈K⁡[X1,…,Xn]f\in K[X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{n}] satisfies K[X1,…,Xn]/(f)≅KK[Y1,…,Yn−1]K[X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{n}]/(f)\cong_{K}K[Y_{1},\ldots\!,Y_{n-1}], then ff is a coordinate.

Last but not least, we present the

Linearization Conjecture: If an automorphism over a field KK with char⁡(K)=0\operatorname{char}(K)=0 has finite order, then it is conjugate to a linear automorphism.

An automorphism that is conjugate to a linear one is called linearizable. For n=2n=2 the (affirmative) answer easily follows from the structure of GA2⁡(K)\operatorname{GA}_{2}(K), which was already observed in [15]. For n≥3n\geq 3 this conjecture is still unsolved. However, we will show (Corollary 4.18) that a linearized polynomial automorphism over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} of finite order relatively prime to qq, is linearizable.

2 Polynomial maps, conventions

Associating a matrix to a polynomial map is a recurring thing in this paper, so first we write down the basic notations used in this paper concerning matrices. Given any commutative ring RR, let Mm×n⁡(R)\operatorname{M}_{m\times n}(R) (or Mn⁡(R)\operatorname{M}_{n}(R), if m=nm=n) be the set of all m×nm\times n matrices with entries in RR. For the group of all invertible matrices in Mn⁡(R)\operatorname{M}_{n}(R) we use the usual notation GLn⁡(R)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(R). InI_{n} will be the identity matrix in GLn⁡(R)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(R).

A polynomial map over KK is a list f=(f1,…,fm)f=(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m}) of polynomials in K⁡[X]K[X]. We can view polynomial maps as KK-algebra homomorphisms K⁡[Y]→K⁡[X]K[Y]\to K[X], Yi↦fiY_{i}\mapsto f_{i}, where Y:=(Y1,…,Ym)Y:=(Y_{1},\ldots\!,Y_{m}) is another list of variables. But they are often also identified with maps Kn→KmK^{n}\to K^{m} given by polynomial substitutions, which is actually only an exact identification if KK is infinite.

Now consider another polynomial map g=(g1,…,gn)g=(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n}), with each gi∈K⁡[Z]g_{i}\in K[Z] for yet another list of variables Z=(Z1,…,Zl)Z=(Z_{1},\ldots\!,Z_{l})\,. In the usual notation, the composition of ff and gg is defined as f∘g=(f1​(g1,…,gn),…,fm​(g1,…,gn))f\circ g=(f_{1}(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n}),\ldots\!,f_{m}(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n})). Restricting to the case m=nm=n, the map ff is called an invertible polynomial map or automorphism if there exists another g=(g1,…,gn)∈K​[X]ng=(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n})\in K[X]^{n} with f∘g=g∘f=Xf\circ g=g\circ f=X (the identity map). Furthermore, we call a polynomial in K⁡[X]K[X] a coordinate if it equals one of the components fif_{i} of some automorphism ff.

The automorphisms form a group, GAn⁡(K)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(K). GLn⁡(K)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) is usually viewed as a subgroup (the subgroup of linear automorphisms), but there are more “usual” subgroups. They will be introduced in this paper where they are needed. As the first and foremost example of associating a matrix to a polynomial map, we write J⁡f\operatorname{J}\!f for the Jacobian matrix (∂fi∂Xj)(\genfrac{}{}{}{1}{\partial f_i}{\partial X_j}) of a polynomial map ff. By the chain rule, for any automorphism ff we have J⁡f∈GLn⁡(K⁡[X])\operatorname{J}\!f\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[X]), whence |J⁡f|∈K∗|\operatorname{J}\!f|\in K^{*}. (Throughout this paper, the operator |⋅||\cdot| takes the determinant of a matrix.)

3 Linearized polynomial maps and the qq-Jacobian

Here we will describe the main objects of study of this paper, and their basic properties. For now, XX denotes just one variable.

Definition 3.1.

Let qq be a positive power of a prime number. Then 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} will be the 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-subspace of 𝔽q​[X]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X] generated by all monomials of the form XqmX^{{}^{q^{m}}} (with m≥0m\geq 0). Furthermore, the composition f∘gf\circ g of f,g∈𝔽q​[X](q)f,g\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} is defined as the substitution of the two polynomials, i.e. (f∘g)​(X):=f⁡(g⁡(X))(f\circ g)(X):=f(g(X)).

Remark 3.2.

The elements of 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} are precisely the polynomials in 𝔽q​[X]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X] that induce an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear map K→KK\to K, where KK is any infinite extension field of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Indeed, XqX^{q} induces the 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear map x↦xq​(x∈K)x\mapsto x^{q}\ (x\in K), and any map induced by an element of 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} is an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear combination of iterates of this particular map. On the other hand, suppose f∈𝔽q​[X]f\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X] induces an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear map K→KK\to K, and let XmX^{m} be a monomial appearing in ff. Since KK is an infinite field, the hypothesis implies that f⁡(X+Y)=f⁡(X)+f⁡(Y)f(X+Y)=f(X)+f(Y) and f⁡(a​X)=a​f​(X)f(aX)=af(X), where YY is a new variable and aa generates the multiplicative group of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Comparing terms of equal degree yields (X+Y)m=Xm+Ym(X+Y)^{m}=X^{m}+Y^{m} and (a​X)m=a​Xm(aX)^{m}=aX^{m}. Let pp be the unique prime number such that q=prq=p^{r}, with r≥1r\geq 1. Suppose mm is not a power of pp, say m=d​pem=dp^{e} with d>1d>1, p∤dp\nmid d and e≥0e\geq 0. Then (X+Y)m=((X+Y)pe)d=(Xpe+Ype)d(X+Y)^{{}^{m}}=((X+Y)^{{}^{p^{e}}})^{{}^{d}}=(X^{{}^{p^{e}}}+Y^{{}^{p^{e}}})^{{}^{d}} contains the nonzero term dX(d−1)​peYpedX^{{}^{(d-1)p^{e}}}Y^{{}^{p^{e}}}, which contradicts the fact that (X+Y)m=Xm+Ym(X+Y)^{m}=X^{m}+Y^{m}. Hence, mm is a power of pp. Since aa generates 𝔽q∗\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} and a∈𝔽ma\in\mathbb{F}_{m} (as am=aa^{m}=a), we have 𝔽q⊆𝔽m\mathbb{F}_{q}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{m}. So 𝔽m\mathbb{F}_{m} is a finite dimensional 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-space, whence mm is a power of qq.

The above remark implies that 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}\, is closed under composition. Moreover, this composition operation has some remarkable properties compared to the composition of any two univariate polynomials over any field (which can be defined in a similar way). For one easily verifies that

  • •

    f⁡(g+h)=f⁡(g)+f⁡(h)∀f,g,h∈𝔽q​[X](q)f(g+h)=f(g)+f(h)\ \ \forall\ f,g,h\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}

  • •

    composition is commutative: f⁡(g⁡(X))=g⁡(f⁡(X))∀f,g∈𝔽q​[X](q)\ f(g(X))=g(f(X))\ \ \forall\ f,g\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}

(The first property follows directly from Remark 3.2.) Using these facts, it is easy to check that 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}\, is a commutative ring (with addition inherited from 𝔽q​[X]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X], and “multiplication” being composition). Also, note that XX is the identity element in this ring, and that 𝔽q→𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}\to\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}\!, a↦a​X\,a\mapsto aX makes 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebra. In fact, Theorem 3.3 will show that 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}\, is isomorphic as 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebra to the univariate polynomial ring over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} !

Here we should remark that linearized polynomials (sometimes referred to as “pp-polynomials” or “qq-polynomials”) have already been studied in several papers. Their focus is mostly on the fact that the roots of a linearized polynomial form an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-subspace of its splitting field (the kernel of the induced linear map). The result of Theorem 3.3 was first mentioned by Ore ([23],[24]). Later, the property mentioned in Remark 3.2 was noted in [5] and [12]. Both properties also appeared in [3],[17] and [18]. However, in this section we will also define multivariate linearized polynomials (the main objects of study of this paper), which have not been studied before in the literature.

Theorem 3.3.

There is a unique isomorphism of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebras δ:𝔽q​[X](q)→𝔽q​[t]\delta:\ \mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}\,\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}[t] such that δ(Xqm)=tm\delta\Big(X^{{}^{q^{m}}}\Big)=\,t^{m} for all m≥0m\geq 0. Thus, δ⁡(f⁡(g))=δ⁡(f)⋅δ⁡(g)∀f,g∈𝔽q​[X](q)\delta(f(g))=\delta(f)\cdot\delta(g)\ \ \forall\ f,g\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}.

Proof.

By the universal property of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebras, there is a unique 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebra homomorphism 𝔽q​[t]→𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]\to\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} such that t↦Xqt\mapsto X^{q}. This map clearly gives a one-to-one correspondence between the 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-bases {tm|m≥0}\{t^{m}\,|\,m\geq 0\} and {Xqm|m≥0}\{X^{{}^{q^{m}}}|\,m\geq 0\}. Hence, the algebra homomorphism is a vector space isomorphism, and thus even an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebra isomorphism (with inverse δ\delta). ∎

Now let X:=(X1,…,Xn)X:=(X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{n}) be a list of variables. Then the polynomials in

𝔽q​[X](q):=𝔽q​[X1](q)⊕⋯⊕𝔽q​[Xn](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}:=\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{1}]^{(q)}\,\oplus\,\cdots\,\oplus\,\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{n}]^{(q)}

are called (multivariate) linearized polynomials in X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots\!,X_{n}. And the elements of (𝔽q​[X](q))m(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{m} (as subset of 𝔽q​[X]m\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{m}) are the (multivariate) linearized polynomial maps.

Remark 3.4.

The elements of 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} are precisely the polynomials in 𝔽q​[X]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X] that induce an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear map Kn→KK^{n}\to K, where KK is any infinite extension field of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Indeed, any term of a given element of 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} is in fact an element of 𝔽q​[Xi](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{i}]^{(q)} for some ii (and the induced map Kn→KK^{n}\to K factorizes through the projection Kn→KK^{n}\to K on the iith factor), so Remark 3.2 implies that elements of 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} induce 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear maps. On the other hand, suppose f∈𝔽q​[X]f\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X] induces an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear map Kn→KK^{n}\to K, and let X1m1⋯XnmnX_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots X_{n}^{m_{n}} be a monomial appearing in ff. As KK is an infinite field, the hypothesis implies that f⁡(X+Y)=f⁡(X)+f⁡(Y)f(X+Y)=f(X)+f(Y), where Y:=(Y1,…,Yn)Y:=(Y_{1},\ldots\!,Y_{n}) is a new list of variables. But then

(X1+Y1)m1⋯(Xn+Yn)mn=X1m1⋯Xnmn+Y1m1⋯Ynmn(X_{1}+Y_{1})^{m_{1}}\cdots(X_{n}+Y_{n})^{m_{n}}=X_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots X_{n}^{m_{n}}+Y_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots Y_{n}^{m_{n}} (1)

since the lefthandside exactly contains all terms X1α1Y1β1⋯XnαnYnβnX_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}Y_{1}^{\beta_{1}}\cdots X_{n}^{\alpha_{n}}Y_{n}^{\beta_{n}} in f⁡(X+Y)f(X+Y) such that αi+βi=mi\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}=m_{i} for all ii. Now suppose we have i≠ji\neq j such that both mi>0m_{i}>0 and mj>0m_{j}>0. Substituting Xi=Yj=0X_{i}=Y_{j}=0 in (1), we get that

Yimi​Xjmj​∏k≠i,j(Xk+Yk)mk=0Y_{i}^{m_{i}}X_{j}^{m_{j}}\prod_{k\neq i,j}(X_{k}+Y_{k})^{m_{k}}=0

which is a contradiction. Thus, only one of the mim_{i} is positive, i.e. the monomial under consideration is a power of one of the XiX_{i}. As a result, f=f1+⋯+fnf=f_{1}+\cdots+f_{n} with fi∈K⁡[Xi]f_{i}\in K[X_{i}] for all ii. We may even assume that f1​(0)=⋯=fn​(0)=0f_{1}(0)=\cdots=f_{n}(0)=0, since the hypothesis on ff implies that it has no constant term. Then each fif_{i} induces an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear map K→KK\to K (the composition of ff and the embedding K→KnK\to K^{n}, α↦α​ei\alpha\mapsto\alpha e_{i}). Remark 3.2 now implies that f∈𝔽q​[X](q)f\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}.

The composition of linearized polynomial maps gives another one: if Z:=(Z1,…,Zl)Z:=(Z_{1},\ldots\!,Z_{l}) is another list of variables, then the composition (already defined for polynomial maps in general) of f=(f1,…,fm)∈(𝔽q​[X](q))mf=(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m})\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{m} and g=(g1,…,gn)∈(𝔽q​[Z](q))ng=(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n})\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[Z]^{(q)})^{n} is the element f∘g=(f1​(g1,…,gn),…,fm​(g1,…,gn))f\circ g=(f_{1}(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n}),\ldots\!,f_{m}(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n})), which can easily be shown to be an element of (𝔽q​[Z](q))m(\mathbb{F}_{q}[Z]^{(q)})^{m}. For the case m=nm=n this implies that (𝔽q​[X](q))n(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n} is closed under composition. Also, Theorem 4.2 will show that GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q):=GAn⁡(𝔽q)∩(𝔽q​[X](q))n\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}:=\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\cap(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n} is a subgroup of GAn⁡(𝔽q)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}).

Theorem 3.7 will show that we can view polynomial maps in (𝔽q​[X](q))m(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{m} as matrices having univariate polynomials over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} as entries. To make this explicit, we define the qq-Jacobian of polynomial maps of this form. The definition is based on certain maps δj\delta_{j} (one for each variable XjX_{j}) that are very similar to the map δ\delta of Theorem 3.3.

Definition 3.5.

Let f=(f1,…,fm)∈(𝔽q​[X](q))mf=(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m})\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{m}, and tt a new variable. For each j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\ldots\!,n\}, let δj:𝔽q​[X](q)→𝔽q​[t]\delta_{j}:\ \mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}\,\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}[t] be the 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-linear map uniquely determined by

δj(Xiqm)={tmi=j0i≠j(m=0,1,2,…)\delta_{j}\left(X_{i}^{{}^{q^{m}}}\right)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}t^{m}&i=j\\ 0&i\neq j\end{array}\right.\ \ \ \ (m=0,1,2,\ldots\,)

Furthermore, we define Jq⁡(f)\operatorname{J}_{q}(f) as the matrix (δj​(fi))∈Mm×n⁡(𝔽q​[t])(\delta_{j}(f_{i}))\in\operatorname{M}_{m\times n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]), and call it the qq-Jacobian of ff (or “J-qq-bian”).

Remark 3.6.

The map

(𝔽q​[X](q))m\displaystyle(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{m} ⟶\displaystyle\longrightarrow Mm×n⁡(𝔽q​[t])\displaystyle\operatorname{M}_{m\times n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t])
(f1,…,fm)\displaystyle(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m}) ↦\displaystyle\mapsto Jq⁡(f)\displaystyle\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)

is obviously one-to-one and onto. We will need this fact henceforth.

Now let g=(g1,…,gn)∈(𝔽q​[Z](q))ng=(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n})\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[Z]^{(q)})^{n}. We will denote the maps 𝔽q​[Z](q)→𝔽q​[t]\mathbb{F}_{q}[Z]^{(q)}\,\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}[t] (similarly defined as the δj\delta_{j}) by εj\varepsilon_{j}. In this situation we have

Theorem 3.7.

If f=(f1,…,fm)∈(𝔽q​[X](q))mf=(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m})\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{m} and g=(g1,…,gn)∈(𝔽q​[Z](q))ng=(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n})\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[Z]^{(q)})^{n}, then Jq⁡(f∘g)=Jq⁡(f)​Jq⁡(g)\operatorname{J}_{q}(f\circ g)=\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)\operatorname{J}_{q}(g).

In particular, Jq\operatorname{J}_{q} induces an isomorphism of 𝔽q\,\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebras (𝔽q​[X](q))n​⟶∼​Mn⁡(𝔽q​[t])\,(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n}\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\operatorname{M}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]).

Proof.

Write fi=∑k=1nfi(k)​(Xk)f_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}f_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X_{k}) and gi=∑r=1lgi(l)​(Zr)g_{i}=\sum_{r=1}^{l}g_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle(l)}(Z_{r}) for all ii. Then

fi​(g)=∑k=1nfi(k)​(gk)=∑k=1nfi(k)​(∑r=1lgk(r)​(Zr))=∑r=1l∑k=1nfi(k)​(gk(r)​(Zr))f_{i}(g)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}f_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(g_{k})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}f_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(\sum_{r=1}^{l}g_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle(r)}(Z_{r}))=\sum_{r=1}^{l}\sum_{k=1}^{n}f_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(g_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle(r)}(Z_{r}))

and thus the (i,j)(i,j)-entry of Jq⁡(f⁡(g))\operatorname{J}_{q}(f(g)) equals

εj​(fi​(g))=εj​(∑k=1nfi(k)​(gk(j)​(Zj)))\displaystyle\varepsilon_{j}(f_{i}(g))=\varepsilon_{j}\,(\sum_{k=1}^{n}f_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(g_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle(j)}(Z_{j}))) =\displaystyle= ∑k=1nεj​(fi(k)​(Zj))⋅εj​(gk(j)​(Zj))\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\,\varepsilon_{j}\,(f_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(Z_{j}))\cdot\varepsilon_{j}\,(g_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle(j)}(Z_{j}))
=\displaystyle= ∑k=1nδk​(fi(k)​(Xk))⋅εj​(gk)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\,\delta_{k}\,(f_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle(k)}(X_{k}))\cdot\varepsilon_{j}\,(g_{k})
=\displaystyle= ∑k=1nδk​(fi)⋅εj​(gk)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\,\delta_{k}\,(f_{i})\cdot\varepsilon_{j}\,(g_{k})

which is exactly equal to the (i,j)(i,j)-entry of the product (δj​(fi))⋅(εj​(gi))(\delta_{j}(f_{i}))\cdot(\varepsilon_{j}(g_{i}))\,. Thus, Jq⁡(f⁡(g))=Jq⁡(f)⋅Jq⁡(g)\operatorname{J}_{q}(f(g))=\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)\cdot\operatorname{J}_{q}(g). The second statement follows from Remark 3.6. ∎

4 The famous problems and conjectures for linearized polynomials

This section is devoted to the solutions that we found for the famous problems and conjectures that were stated in the Introduction, for the cases where the involved polynomials are linearized polynomials.

4.1 Tame Generators Problem and Jacobian Conjecture

Before solving the Tame Generators Problem for linearized polynomial maps, we recall the concept of tameness.

Definition 4.1.

EAn⁡(K)\operatorname{EA}_{n}(K) (for any field KK) is the subgroup of GAn⁡(K)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(K) generated by the elementary automorphisms. An elementary automorphism is one of the form (X1,…,Xi−1,Xi+fi,Xi+1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{i-1},X_{i}+f_{i},X_{i+1},\ldots\!,X_{n}) for some ii, where fi∈K⁡[X^i]f_{i}\in K[\hat{X}_{i}]. Furthermore, TAn⁡(K)\operatorname{TA}_{n}(K), the group of tame automorphisms, is the subgroup generated by GLn⁡(K)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) and EAn⁡(K)\operatorname{EA}_{n}(K).

As mentioned in the Introduction, the question which automorphisms are tame is still open in general if n≥3n\geq 3. However, Theorem 4.2 will show that all invertible linearized polynomial maps are tame. To formulate the precise statement, we need to define a few automorphism subgroups consisting of linearized polynomial maps. First, we put

EAn(𝔽q)(q):=⟨(X1,…,Xi−1,Xi+fi,Xi+1,…,Xn)| 1≤i≤n,fi∈𝔽q[X^i](q)⟩\operatorname{EA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}:=\langle\,(X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{i-1},X_{i}+f_{i},X_{i+1},\ldots\!,X_{n})\,|\,1\leq i\leq n,f_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[\hat{X}_{i}]^{(q)}\,\rangle

Furthermore, let TAn⁡(𝔽q)(q):=⟨EAn⁡(𝔽q)(q),GLn⁡(𝔽q)⟩\operatorname{TA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}:=\langle\,\operatorname{EA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}\,,\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\,\rangle. Under the isomorphism of Theorem 3.7, the subgroup EAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)\operatorname{EA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} corresponds to En⁡(𝔽q​[t])\operatorname{E}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]), the subgroup of GLn⁡(𝔽q​[t])\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]) generated by all elementary matrices. Also, this isomorphism is the identity on GLn⁡(𝔽q)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}).

Theorem 4.2.

Let f=(f1,…,fm)∈(𝔽q​[X](q))mf=(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m})\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{m}. Then there exist h1∈TAm⁡(𝔽q)(q)h_{1}\in\operatorname{TA}_{m}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} and h2∈TAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)h_{2}\in\operatorname{TA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} such that h1​f​h2h_{1}fh_{2} is a “diagonal map”, i.e. a map of the form g=(g1,…,gm)g=(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{m}), where gi∈𝔽q​[Xi](q)g_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{i}]^{(q)} for all ii (and gi=0g_{i}=0 if m>nm>n and n<i≤mn<i\leq m).

Furthermore, GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)=TAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}=\operatorname{TA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}.

Proof.

Jq⁡(f)\operatorname{J}_{q}(f) is a matrix over a Euclidean domain, so there exist M∈GLm⁡(𝔽q​[t])M\in\operatorname{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]) (=⟨Em⁡(𝔽q​[t]),GLm⁡(𝔽q)⟩)(\,=\nolinebreak\!\langle\operatorname{E}_{m}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]),\operatorname{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\rangle\,) and N∈GLn⁡(𝔽q​[t])N\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]) such that M​Jq​(f)​NM\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)N is a (in general non-square) diagonal matrix. By Remark 3.6, there exist h1∈TAm⁡(𝔽q)(q)h_{1}\in\operatorname{TA}_{m}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} and h2∈TAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)h_{2}\in\operatorname{TA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} such that h1​f​h2h_{1}fh_{2} is of the prescribed form. For the next statement, suppose f∈GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)f\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}. The above says that ff is tamely equivalent to a map g=(g1,…,gn)g=(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n}) with gi∈𝔽q​[Xi](q)g_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{i}]^{(q)}\, for all ii. Since ff is an automorphism, gg is too, so let h=(h1,…,hn)∈GAn⁡(𝔽q)h=(h_{1},\ldots\!,h_{n})\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) be the inverse of gg. Since 𝔽q​[X1,…,Xi−1,Xi+1,…,Xn]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{i-1},X_{i+1},\ldots\!,X_{n}] is a domain, the equations gi​(hi​(X))=Xig_{i}(h_{i}(X))=X_{i} imply that hi∈𝔽q​[Xi]h_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{i}] and that both gig_{i} and hih_{i} have degree 1 (for all ii). Consequently, f∈TAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)f\in\operatorname{TA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}. ∎

Note that this theorem in particular implies that f−1∈GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)f^{-1}\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} if f∈GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)f\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}, i.e. GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} is a subgroup of GAn⁡(𝔽q)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}). As a result, we can affirm an analogue of the Jacobian Conjecture for linearized polynomial maps and their qq-Jacobians.

Corollary 4.3.

f∈(𝔽q​[X](q))nf\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n} is an automorphism if and only if Jq⁡(f)∈GLn⁡(𝔽q​[t])\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]).

Proof.

This follows from Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 4.2: if f∈GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)f\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} then f−1∈GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)f^{-1}\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} and Jq⁡(f)​Jq⁡(f−1)=Jq⁡(f​f−1)=In\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)\operatorname{J}_{q}(f^{-1})=\operatorname{J}_{q}(ff^{-1})=I_{n}. If on the other hand Jq⁡(f)∈GLn⁡(𝔽q​[t])\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]), let g∈(𝔽q​[X](q))ng\in(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n} such that Jq⁡(g)=(Jq⁡(f))−1\operatorname{J}_{q}(g)=(\operatorname{J}_{q}(f))^{-1} (which exists by Remark 3.6). Then Jq⁡(f​g)=Jq⁡(f)​Jq⁡(g)=In\operatorname{J}_{q}(fg)=\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)\operatorname{J}_{q}(g)=I_{n} implies that ff is an automorphism with inverse gg. ∎

Note that if we take the usual Jacobian, the statement doesn’t hold; namely, the Jacobian of any linearized polynomial map equals the Jacobian of its linear part.

4.2 Coordinate Recognition Problem

Corollary 4.3 provides us with the following useful tool: a criterion to decide whether a linearized polynomial is a coordinate.

Proposition 4.4.

For f1∈𝔽q​[X](q)f_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}\,, the following are equivalent.

  1. 1.

    f1f_{1} is a coordinate of an automorphism in 𝔽q​[X]n\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{n}

  2. 2.

    f1f_{1} is a coordinate of an automorphism in (𝔽q​[X](q))n(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n}

  3. 3.

    (δ1​(f1),…,δn​(f1))=(1)(\delta_{1}(f_{1}),\ldots\!,\delta_{n}(f_{1}))=(1) in 𝔽q​[t]\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]

Proof of the equivalence of 2. and 3..

f1f_{1} is a coordinate in (𝔽q​[X](q))n(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n} if and only if (δ1​(f1),…,δn​(f1))(\delta_{1}(f_{1}),\ldots\!,\delta_{n}(f_{1})) is a row that is extendible to a matrix in GLn⁡(𝔽q​[t])\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]) if and only if (δ1​(f1),…,δn​(f1))=(1)(\delta_{1}(f_{1}),\ldots\!,\delta_{n}(f_{1}))=(1) in 𝔽q​[t]\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]. (We use Remark 3.6 again.) ∎

From this we obtain the remarkable fact (Corollary 4.5) that all prime power polynomials are essentially univariate (i.e., up to a polynomial transformation). This fact in turn will help us complete the proof of Proposition 4.4.

Corollary 4.5.

Every element of 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} is a linearized polynomial in a coordinate of an automorphism in (𝔽q​[X](q))n(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n}.

Proof.

Let f∈𝔽q​[X](q)f\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}, and h:=gcd⁡(δ1​(f),…,δn​(f))∈𝔽q​[t]h:=\gcd(\delta_{1}(f),\ldots\!,\delta_{n}(f))\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[t] (unique if we assume hh to be a monic polynomial). Then we have (δ1​(f),…,δn​(f))=(h)(\delta_{1}(f),\ldots\!,\delta_{n}(f))=(h) (as ideals in 𝔽q​[t]\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]), and we can write δi​(f)=h​gi\delta_{i}(f)=hg_{i} with g1,…,gn∈𝔽q​[t]g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[t]. Now let fi~∈𝔽q​[Xi](q)​(i=1,…,n)\tilde{f_{i}}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{i}]^{(q)}\ (i=1,\ldots\!,n) and h~∈𝔽q​[X1](q)\tilde{h}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{1}]^{(q)} such that δi​(fi~)=gi​(t)\delta_{i}(\tilde{f_{i}})=g_{i}(t) and Jq⁡(h~)=h⁡(t)\operatorname{J}_{q}(\tilde{h})=h(t) (using Remark 3.6 again). Then f~:=f1~+⋯+fn~\tilde{f}:=\tilde{f_{1}}+\cdots+\tilde{f_{n}} gives

Jq(f)=(δ1(f)⋯δn(f))=(hg1⋯hgn)=h⋅(g1⋯gn)=Jq(h~)Jq(f~)=Jq(h~(f~))\operatorname{J}_{q}(f)=(\delta_{1}(f)\ \cdots\ \delta_{n}(f))=(hg_{1}\ \cdots\ hg_{n})=h\cdot(g_{1}\ \cdots\ g_{n})=\operatorname{J}_{q}(\tilde{h})\operatorname{J}_{q}(\tilde{f})=\operatorname{J}_{q}(\tilde{h}(\tilde{f}))

Hence, f=h~​(f~)f=\tilde{h}(\tilde{f}), and (δ1​(f~),…,δn​(f~))=(g1,…,gn)=(1)(\delta_{1}(\tilde{f}),\ldots\!,\delta_{n}(\tilde{f}))=(g_{1},\ldots\!,g_{n})=(1) in 𝔽q​[t]\mathbb{F}_{q}[t], so f~\tilde{f} is a coordinate by the equivalence of 2. and 3. in Proposition 4.4. ∎

Proof of the equivalence of 1. and 2.(Proposition 4.4).

The only nontrivial implication is 1.⇒\,\Rightarrow\,2., so assume that f1f_{1} is a coordinate of an automorphism in 𝔽q​[X]n\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{n}. By Corollary 4.5, f1=g1​(h1)f_{1}=g_{1}(h_{1}) with g1∈𝔽q​[X1](q)g_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{1}]^{(q)} and h1∈𝔽q​[X](q)h_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}, and such that h1h_{1} is the first coordinate of an automorphism in (𝔽q​[X](q))n(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n}. Applying the inverse of this automorphism to f1f_{1}, we deduce that g1​(X1)g_{1}(X_{1}) is a coordinate as well. Just as in the proof of Theorem 4.2, this implies that g1g_{1} has degree 1, say g1​(X1)=a​X1+bg_{1}(X_{1})=aX_{1}+b with a∈𝔽q∗a\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{\,*} and b∈𝔽qb\in\mathbb{F}_{q}. But g1∈𝔽q​[X1](q)g_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{1}]^{(q)}, so b=0b=0. Now f1=a​h1f_{1}=ah_{1} is the first coordinate of an automorphism in (𝔽q​[X](q))n(\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)})^{n}. ∎

One can write down many coordinates over finite fields of such a form, that they can’t possibly be coordinates when considered over a field of characteristic zero. This is illustrated in the following example. A polynomial as described there, i.e. of the form f~:=f⁡(X)+Yqn\tilde{f}:=f(X)+Y^{q^{n}}, can only be a coordinate over a characteristic zero field KK in the trivial cases n=0n=0 or ff has degree 1 (as will follow from Proposition 5.12).

Example 4.6.

Any element of 𝔽q​[X,Y](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X,Y]^{(q)} (two variables) of the form f⁡(X)+Yqnf(X)+Y^{q^{n}}, with n≥0n\geq 0 and linear part of ff equal to XX, is a coordinate. Namely, let g⁡(X):=f⁡(X)−X∈𝔽q​[X](q)g(X):=f(X)-X\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}. Note that g⁡(X)=h​(X)qg(X)=h(X)^{q} for some h∈𝔽q​[X](q)h\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} (for gg contains no linear term), whence g^​(t):=δ1​(g⁡(X))=δ1​(Xq)​δ1​(h⁡(X))=t​h^​(t)\hat{g}(t):=\delta_{1}(g(X))=\delta_{1}(X^{q})\delta_{1}(h(X))=t\hat{h}(t), where h^​(t):=δ1​(h⁡(X))\hat{h}(t):=\delta_{1}(h(X)). Thus,

(1+g^​(t)tn(−1)n+1​h^​(t)n1−(−g^​(t))n1−(−g^​(t)))∈GL2⁡(𝔽q​[t])\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1+\hat{g}(t)&t^{n}\\ (-1)^{n+1}\hat{h}(t)^{n}&\tfrac{1-(-\hat{g}(t))^{n}}{1-(-\hat{g}(t))}\end{array}\right)\in\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t])

(f⁡(X)+Yqn,(−1)n+1​h​(X)(n)+∑k=0n−1(−1)k​g​(Y)(k))∈GA2⁡(𝔽q)(f(X)+Y^{q^{n}},(-1)^{n+1}h(X)^{(n)}+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{k}g(Y)^{(k)})\in\operatorname{GA}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{q})

where each exponent “(k)(k)” of a polynomial denotes kk-fold composition of that polynomial with itself (and g​(Y)(0):=Yg(Y)^{(0)}:=Y). In particular, h⁡(X):=Xqm−1h(X):=X^{q^{m-1}} (m≥1m\geq 1) gives

(X+Xqm+Yqn,(−1)n+1​Xq(m−1)​n+∑k=0n−1(−1)k​Yqk​m)∈GA2⁡(𝔽q)(X+X^{q^{m}}+Y^{q^{n}},(-1)^{n+1}X^{q^{(m-1)n}}+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{k}Y^{q^{km}})\in\operatorname{GA}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{q})

Assuming m,n≥2m,n\geq 2, and writing n=r​m+sn=rm+s with r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} and 0≤s≤m−10\leq s\leq m-1, we can also complete this automorphism using a polynomial of lower degree. Namely,

(X+Xqm+Yqn,(−1)r​Xqm−s+∑k=0r(−1)k​Yqk​m)∈GA2⁡(𝔽q)(X+X^{q^{m}}+Y^{q^{n}},(-1)^{r}X^{q^{m-s}}+\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^{k}Y^{q^{km}})\in\operatorname{GA}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{q})

since

(1+tmtn(−1)r​tm−s1−(−tm)r+11−(−tm))∈GL2⁡(𝔽q​[t])\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1+t^{m}&t^{n}\\ (-1)^{r}t^{m-s}&\tfrac{1-(-t^{m})^{r+1}}{1-(-t^{m})}\end{array}\right)\in\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[t])

4.3 Polynomial Ring Recognition Problem and Abhyankar-Sathaye Conjecture

A finitely generated KK-algebra AA can be represented as A=K⁡[X]/IA=K[X]/I, where II is an ideal of K⁡[X]K[X]. A necessary condition for being a polynomial ring over KK is that AA is a domain, whence II must be a prime ideal. If KK is a finite field and II is generated by linearized polynomials, we will show that the condition of being a domain is actually also sufficient (Corollary 4.10). This differs significantly from the characteristic zero case, which has only been solved in case XX represents at most two variables. We will first summarize the results of this case.

To begin, if II is even a maximal ideal, then K⁡[X]/IK[X]/I is a field, which is of course only a polynomial ring over KK if it equals KK (the units of both fields must coincide). In other words, the canonical embedding K→K⁡[X]/IK\to K[X]/I is actually an isomorphism. In this case, choosing a1,…,an∈Ka_{1},\ldots\!,a_{n}\in K such that Xi−ai∈IX_{i}-a_{i}\in I for all ii (which exist since the embedding is onto), we get that I=(X1−a1,…,Xn−an)I=(X_{1}-a_{1},\ldots\!,X_{n}-a_{n}). So in case of a maximal ideal II, AA is a polynomial ring if and only if II is of this form.

This also solves the general case n=1n=1, since any nonzero prime ideal of K⁡[X]K[X] is then maximal. And in the case of two variables, any non-maximal, nonzero prime ideal of K⁡[X]K[X] is generated by one irreducible polynomial (since K⁡[X]K[X] is a factorial ring). Hence, the following result, proved by Abhyankar and Moh in [1] and independently by Suzuki in [27], completes the solution of the two-variable Polynomial Ring Recognition Problem over a field of characteristic zero.

Theorem 4.7 (Abhyankar-Moh-Suzuki).

Let KK a field with char⁡(K)=0\operatorname{char}(K)=0. If a polynomial f1∈K⁡[X,Y]f_{1}\in K[X,Y] satisfies K[X,Y]/(f1)≅KK[Z]K[X,Y]/(f_{1})\cong_{K}K[Z], then f1f_{1} is a coordinate.

Contrary to the characteristic zero case, several counterexamples to Theorem 4.7 have been found in characteristic p>0p>0. Here is one which was also mentioned in [20].

Example 4.8.

Take any prime number p>2p>2, and let f1:=Yp2−X2​p−Xf_{1}:=Y^{p^{2}}-X^{2p}-X. Then 𝔽p​[X,Y]/(f1)≅𝔽p​[T]\mathbb{F}_{p}[X,Y]/(f_{1})\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}[T], where TT is a variable; this isomorphism is induced by φ:𝔽p​[X,Y]→𝔽p​[T],X↦Tp2,Y↦T2​p+T\varphi:\ \mathbb{F}_{p}[X,Y]\to\mathbb{F}_{p}[T],\ X\mapsto T^{p^{2}},Y\mapsto T^{2p}+T. But we claim that f1f_{1} is not a coordinate.

First, note that φ\varphi is indeed surjective since f2:=Y−(Yp−X2)2f_{2}:=Y-(Y^{p}-X^{2})^{2} satisfies φ⁡(f2)=T\varphi(f_{2})=T. Now we show that Ker⁡(φ)=(f1)\operatorname{Ker}(\varphi)=(f_{1}). Since the (Krull) dimensions of 𝔽p​[X,Y]\mathbb{F}_{p}[X,Y] and 𝔽p​[T]\mathbb{F}_{p}[T] are equal to 2 resp. 1, Ker⁡(φ)\operatorname{Ker}(\varphi) must be a height 1 prime ideal, and thus a principal ideal due to the factoriality of 𝔽p​[X,Y]\mathbb{F}_{p}[X,Y]. So it suffices to show that f1f_{1} is irreducible over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. So let β\beta be an element of an extension field of K:=𝔽p​(X)K:=\mathbb{F}_{p}(X) such that βp2=α:=X2​p+X\beta^{p^{2}}=\alpha:=X^{2p}+X. Then f1=Yp2−α=(Y−β)p2f_{1}=Y^{p^{2}}-\alpha=(Y-\beta)^{p^{2}} over K⁡(β)K(\beta). Let 1≤m≤p21\leq m\leq p^{2} be minimal such that (Y−β)m∈K⁡[Y](Y-\beta)^{m}\in K[Y]. Then (Y−β)m(Y-\beta)^{m} is irreducible over KK, and in fact the only irreducible factor of f1f_{1} (since two positive powers of Y−βY-\beta cannot be coprime). Hence f1f_{1} is a power of (Y−β)m(Y-\beta)^{m}, and m|p2m\mid p^{2}. Now suppose m=1m=1 or m=pm=p. Then Yp−βp=(Y−β)p∈K⁡[Y]Y^{p}-\beta^{p}=(Y-\beta)^{p}\in K[Y], so α=(βp)p∈Kp=𝔽p​(Xp)\alpha=(\beta^{p})^{p}\in K^{p}=\mathbb{F}_{p}(X^{p}), a contradiction. As a result, m=p2m=p^{2}, and the conclusion is that f1f_{1} is irreducible over KK.

Now suppose f1f_{1} is a coordinate. Using the fact that 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} is a field, Corollary 5.1.6 in [10] yields an f2′∈𝔽p​[X,Y]f_{2}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[X,Y] with deg⁡(f2′)<deg⁡(f1)\deg(f_{2}^{\prime})<\deg(f_{1}) and (f1,f2′)∈GA2⁡(𝔽p)(f_{1},f_{2}^{\prime})\in\operatorname{GA}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p}). (Here “deg\deg” denotes the (total) degree of a polynomial.) Since 𝔽p​[X,Y]/(f1)=𝔽p​[f1,f2′]/(f1)=𝔽p​[f2′¯]\mathbb{F}_{p}[X,Y]/(f_{1})=\mathbb{F}_{p}[f_{1},f_{2}^{\prime}]/(f_{1})=\mathbb{F}_{p}[\overline{f_{2}^{\prime}}] (f2′¯\overline{f_{2}^{\prime}} being the equivalence class of f2′f_{2}^{\prime} modulo (f1)(f_{1})), we must have 𝔽p​[φ⁡(f2′)]=𝔽p​[T]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\varphi(f_{2}^{\prime})]=\mathbb{F}_{p}[T], whence φ⁡(f2′)=a​T+b\varphi(f_{2}^{\prime})=aT+b with a∈𝔽p∗,b∈𝔽pa\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*},b\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. But φ⁡(f2)=T\varphi(f_{2})=T, which implies that f2′−a​f2−b∈Ker⁡(φ)=(f1)f_{2}^{\prime}-af_{2}-b\in\operatorname{Ker}(\varphi)=(f_{1}). From deg⁡(f2′−a​f2−b)<deg⁡(f1)\deg(f_{2}^{\prime}-af_{2}-b)<\deg(f_{1}) we now conclude that f2′−a​f2−b=0f_{2}^{\prime}-af_{2}-b=0. Thus, (f1,f2)∈GA2⁡(𝔽p)(f_{1},f_{2})\in\operatorname{GA}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p}). But according to Corollary 5.1.6 in [10] either deg⁡(f1)|deg⁡(f2)\deg(f_{1})\mid\deg(f_{2}) or deg⁡(f2)|deg⁡(f1)\deg(f_{2})\mid\deg(f_{1}), contradicting the fact that deg⁡(f1)=p2\deg(f_{1})=p^{2} and deg⁡(f2)=2​p\deg(f_{2})=2p.

Theorem 4.9 is the key to the solution of the Polynomial Ring Recognition Problem for 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebras which are defined by linearized polynomials (Corollary 4.10).

Theorem 4.9.

Let 𝔭\mathfrak{p} be a prime ideal in 𝔽q​[X]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X] generated by linearized polynomials. Then these polynomials can be chosen in such a way that together they are extendible to an automorphism in GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}.

More generally, let 𝔞\mathfrak{a} be any ideal in 𝔽q​[X]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X] generated by linearized polynomials. Then there exist h=(h1,…,hn)∈GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)h=(h_{1},\ldots\!,h_{n})\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)}, r≤nr\leq n and gi∈𝔽q​[Xi](q)\{0}g_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{i}]^{(q)}\backslash\{0\} for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots\!,r, such that 𝔞=(g1​(h1),…,gr​(hr))\mathfrak{a}=(g_{1}(h_{1}),\ldots\!,g_{r}(h_{r})).

For i∈{1,…,r}i\in\{1,\ldots\!,r\} we write gi​(Xi)=Xiei​gi~​(Xi)g_{i}(X_{i})=X_{i}^{e_{i}}\tilde{g_{i}}(X_{i}) with gi~∈𝔽q​[Xi]\tilde{g_{i}}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{i}], gi~​(0)≠0\tilde{g_{i}}(0)\neq 0 and ei>0e_{i}>0 (note that gi∈𝔽q​[Xi](q)g_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{i}]^{(q)}, so indeed gi∈(Xi)g_{i}\in(X_{i})). Since g0​(0)=0g_{0}(0)=0 for all g0∈𝔭g_{0}\in\mathfrak{p}, we must have gi~​(Xi)∉𝔭\tilde{g_{i}}(X_{i})\notin\mathfrak{p}, whence Xi∈𝔭X_{i}\in\mathfrak{p} (since 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is a prime ideal). Substituting Xj:=0X_{j}:=0 for all j≠ij\neq i, we obtain Xi∈(Xiei​gi~​(Xi))X_{i}\in(X_{i}^{e_{i}}\tilde{g_{i}}(X_{i})). This implies that ei=1e_{i}=1 and gi~​(Xi)∈𝔽q∗\tilde{g_{i}}(X_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. Consequently, 𝔭=(X1,…,Xr)\mathfrak{p}=(X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{r}).

Now we prove the second statement. First note that 𝔞\mathfrak{a} is generated by finitely many linearized polynomials. Namely, 𝔞\mathfrak{a} is generated by finitely many general polynomials (since 𝔞\mathfrak{a} is an ideal in a Noetherian ring), and each of these general polynomials can be written as an 𝔽q​[X]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]-linear combination of finitely many of the linearized polynomials that generate 𝔞\mathfrak{a}. So let 𝔞=(f1,…,fm)\mathfrak{a}=(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m}) for some m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and f1,…,fm∈𝔽q​[X](q)f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)}. Since

and thus 𝔞=(f1,…,fm)=(h~1​(f),…,h~m​(f))\mathfrak{a}=(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{m})=(\tilde{h}_{1}(f),\ldots\!,\tilde{h}_{m}(f)). ∎

Corollary 4.10.

Let A=𝔽q​[X]/IA=\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]/I be a finitely generated 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebra, where II is an ideal in 𝔽q​[X]\mathbb{F}_{q}[X] generated by linearized polynomials. Then AA is (isomorphic to) a polynomial ring over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} if and only if AA is a domain.

Theorem 4.7 relates the Polynomial Ring Recognition Problem to the Coordinate Recognition Problem for the case of two variables. But this connection is in fact more general. Namely, it is easily seen, that if f1∈K⁡[X1,…,Xn]f_{1}\in K[X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{n}] is a coordinate, then the KK-algebra K⁡[X1,…,Xn]/(f1)K[X_{1},\ldots\!,X_{n}]/(f_{1}) is a polynomial ring over KK in n−1n-1 variables. The reverse statement is the Abhyankar-Sathaye Conjecture, which in case n=2n=2 has an affirmative answer by Theorem 4.7. Although the Abhyankar-Sathaye Conjecture is false in nonzero characteristic in general (as shown in Example 4.8), the statement holds for linearized polynomials:

Theorem 4.11.

If f1∈𝔽q​[X](q)f_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} satisfies 𝔽q[X]/(f1)≅𝔽q𝔽q[Y1,…,Yn−1]\,\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]/(f_{1})\cong_{\,\mathbb{F}_{q}}\mathbb{F}_{q}[Y_{1},\ldots\!,Y_{n-1}], then f1f_{1} is a coordinate.

Proof.

According to Corollary 4.5, f1=g1​(h1)f_{1}=g_{1}(h_{1}), where h1h_{1} is a coordinate in 𝔽q​[X](q)\mathbb{F}_{q}[X]^{(q)} and g1∈𝔽q​[X1](q)g_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[X_{1}]^{(q)}. Then g1​(0)=0g_{1}(0)=0, so h1h_{1} divides f1f_{1}. Additionally, (f1)(f_{1}) is a prime ideal (as 𝔽q​[Y1,…,Yn−1]\mathbb{F}_{q}[Y_{1},\ldots\!,Y_{n-1}] is a domain), whence f1=c​h1f_{1}=ch_{1} for some c∈𝔽q∗c\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. Thus, f1f_{1} is a coordinate. ∎

4.4 Linearization Conjecture

The Linearization Conjecture doesn’t hold in general in positive characteristic, which is demonstrated in the following example. Throughout this section, XX (and also YY) denotes one variable.

Example 4.12.

f:=(X+Y2,Y)∈GA2⁡(𝔽2)f:=(X+Y^{2},Y)\in\operatorname{GA}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{2}) has order 2, but is not linearizable. This already follows from two obvious facts about ff: its linear part equals the identity, and f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0. Namely, suppose g∈GA2⁡(𝔽2)g\in\operatorname{GA}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{2}) such that g​f​g−1=l∈GL2⁡(𝔽2)gfg^{-1}=l\in\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{2}), and let c:=g⁡(0)c:=g(0). Then g~:=(X−c1,Y−c2)∘g\tilde{g}:=(X-c_{1},Y-c_{2})\circ g satisfies g~​(0)=0\tilde{g}(0)=0, and

g~​f​g~−1=(X−c1,Y−c2)​l​(X+c1,Y+c2)\tilde{g}f\tilde{g}^{-1}=(X-c_{1},Y-c_{2})l(X+c_{1},Y+c_{2}) (2)

Since ff and g~\tilde{g} have zero constant part, we can find the linear part of the lefthandside of (2) by composing the linear parts of the factors of this composition. Hence, the linear part of the lefthandside equals the identity. Looking at the righthandside of (2), we conclude that l=(X,Y)l=(X,Y). But then also f=(X,Y)f=(X,Y), a contradiction.

In view of this example, a question arises: is the Linearization Conjecture true in nonzero characteristic if we additionally assume that the characteristic doesn’t divide the order of the automorphism? For linearized polynomial maps, this question has an affirmative answer (Corollary 4.18). Because of Theorem 3.7, the proof of this fact involves matrices in GLn⁡(K⁡[t])\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[t]) satisfying a polynomial relation over KK.

Lemma 4.13.

Let RR be a domain containing a field KK, such that KK is integrally closed in LL, the field of fractions of RR. Furthermore, let h⁡(X)∈R⁡[X]h(X)\in R[X] be the characteristic polynomial of a given A∈GLn⁡(R)A\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(R), and g⁡(X)∈L⁡[X]g(X)\in L[X] the minimal polynomial of AA over LL. Suppose f⁡(A)=0f(A)=0 for some f⁡(X)∈K⁡[X]f(X)\in K[X]. Then also g⁡(X),h⁡(X)∈K⁡[X]g(X),h(X)\in K[X].

Proof.

g⁡(X)g(X) divides f⁡(X)f(X) in L⁡[X]L[X]. Let L′L^{\prime} be a splitting field of ff over LL. Since f⁡(X)∈K⁡[X]f(X)\in K[X], the roots of ff in L′L^{\prime} (and in particular those of gg) are integral over KK, whence the coefficients of gg are too. Moreover, h⁡(X)h(X) has the same roots as g⁡(X)g(X), so the coefficients of hh are integral over KK as well. But KK is integrally closed in LL, so g⁡(X),h⁡(X)∈K⁡[X]g(X),h(X)\in K[X]. ∎

Theorem 4.15.

Let A∈GLn⁡(K⁡[t])A\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[t]) such that its minimal polynomial g⁡(X)g(X) over K⁡(t)K(t) is an irreducible polynomial in K⁡[X]K[X] of degree d≥1d\geq 1.

  1. 1.

    If gg is separable over KK, then AA is conjugate (over K⁡[t]K[t]) to the n×nn\times n block diagonal matrix where each block is the companion matrix of gg.

  2. 2.

    If d=nd=n then AA is conjugate (over K⁡[t]K[t]) to the companion matrix of gg.

Proof.

The characteristic polynomial of AA (an element of K⁡[X]K[X] by Lemma 4.13) must be a power of gg, say gmg^{m} with m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*} such that n=d​mn=dm. Write g⁡(X)=Xd+cd−1​Xd−1+⋯+c1​X+c0g(X)=X^{d}+c_{d-1}X^{d-1}+\cdots+c_{1}X+c_{0}, where ci∈Kc_{i}\in K for all ii. Moreover, let LL denote the splitting field of gg over KK. Also, we use the following notation: if K1⊆K2K_{1}\subseteq K_{2} are fields and M∈Mn⁡(K1​[t])M\in\operatorname{M}_{n}(K_{1}[t]), then KerK2⁡(M)\operatorname{Ker}_{K_{2}}(M) denotes the kernel of the endomorphism of K2​[t]nK_{2}[t]^{n} induced by MM. This kernel is then viewed as a K2​[t]K_{2}[t]-module. Furthermore, M⊤M^{\top} denotes the transpose of any matrix MM.

First, assume that gg is separable over KK. Then gg has dd distinct roots in LL. Furthermore, L/KL/K is a Galois extension, say with Galois group GG. Since LL is the splitting field of an irreducible polynomial over KK, GG acts transitively on the roots of gg. Therefore, we can find σ1,σ2,…,σd∈G\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots\!,\sigma_{d}\in G (with σ1\sigma_{1} the identity map) and α∈L\alpha\in L such that σ1​(α),…,σd​(α)\sigma_{1}(\alpha),\ldots\!,\sigma_{d}(\alpha) are the roots of gg in LL. Then KerL⁡(A−σi​(α)​I)=σi~​(KerL⁡(A−α​I))\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\sigma_{i}(\alpha)I)=\tilde{\sigma_{i}}(\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\alpha I)), where the automorphism σi~\tilde{\sigma_{i}} is the natural extension of σi\sigma_{i} to L​[t]nL[t]^{n} (preserving tt). As a result, KerL⁡(A−σ1​(α)​I),…,KerL⁡(A−σd​(α)​I)\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\sigma_{1}(\alpha)I),\ldots\!,\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\sigma_{d}(\alpha)I) all have the same rank as free L⁡[t]L[t]-modules. (Note that indeed they are all free modules, being submodules of a finite free module over a principal ideal domain.) Moreover, from Proposition 4.14 (over L⁡[t]L[t] instead of K⁡[t]K[t]) we learn that L​[t]n=KerL⁡(A−σ1​(α)​I)⊕⋯⊕KerL⁡(A−σd​(α)​I)L[t]^{n}=\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\sigma_{1}(\alpha)I)\oplus\cdots\oplus\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\sigma_{d}(\alpha)I). Consequently, the rank of KerL⁡(A−σi​(α)​I)\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\sigma_{i}(\alpha)I) equals mm for all ii.

Again by Proposition 4.14 (and using the fact that gg is separable over KK), we know that KerK⁡(α)⁡(A−α​I)\operatorname{Ker}_{K(\alpha)}(A-\alpha I) is a direct summand of K⁡(α)​[t]nK(\alpha)[t]^{n}. Also, tensoring with a free (and thus flat) module preserves kernels, so we have L⊗K⁡(α)KerK⁡(α)⁡(A−α​I)=KerL⁡(A−α​I)L\otimes_{K(\alpha)}\operatorname{Ker}_{K(\alpha)}(A-\alpha I)=\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\alpha I). Hence, since KerK⁡(α)⁡(A−α​I)\operatorname{Ker}_{K(\alpha)}(A-\alpha I) is a free K​(α)​[t]K(\alpha)[t]-module, its rank over K​(α)​[t]K(\alpha)[t] is equal to the rank of KerL⁡(A−α​I)\operatorname{Ker}_{L}(A-\alpha I) over L⁡[t]L[t], which is mm.

Let {v1,…,vm}\{v_{1},\ldots\!,v_{m}\} be a basis of KerK⁡(α)⁡(A−α​I)\operatorname{Ker}_{K(\alpha)}(A-\alpha I). Let B∈Mn×m⁡(K⁡(α)​[t])B\in\operatorname{M}_{n\times m}(K(\alpha)[t]) be the matrix with v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots\!,v_{m} as its columns, which satisfies A​B=α​BAB=\alpha B. Note that then

Mn⁡(K⁡(α)​[t])​B=∑i=0d−1Mn⁡(K⁡[t])​αi​B=∑i=0d−1Mn⁡(K⁡[t])​Ai​B⊆Mn⁡(K⁡[t])​B\operatorname{M}_{n}(K(\alpha)[t])B=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{M}_{n}(K[t])\alpha^{i}B=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{M}_{n}(K[t])A^{i}B\subseteq\operatorname{M}_{n}(K[t])B

whence Mn⁡(K⁡(α)​[t])​B=Mn⁡(K⁡[t])​B\operatorname{M}_{n}(K(\alpha)[t])B=\operatorname{M}_{n}(K[t])B. Since v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots\!,v_{m} are the first mm elements of a basis of K⁡(α)​[t]nK(\alpha)[t]^{n}, BB can be completed to an invertible n×nn\times n matrix over K​(α)​[t]K(\alpha)[t]. Taking together the first mm rows of its inverse, we obtain a B′∈Mm×n⁡(K⁡(α)​[t])B^{\prime}\in\operatorname{M}_{m\times n}(K(\alpha)[t]) such that B′​B=ImB^{\prime}B=I_{m}. Now define

where eα:=(1α⋯αd−1)⊤e_{\alpha}:=(1\ \alpha\,\cdots\,\alpha^{d-1})^{\top} and each “00” is a column consisting of dd zeroes. For every n′≥1n^{\prime}\geq 1 this gives an isomorphism of K⁡[t]K[t]-modules

In particular, there exists a D∈Mn⁡(K⁡[t])D\in\operatorname{M}_{n}(K[t]) such that D​Eα=BDE_{\alpha}=B. But we claim that even D∈GLn⁡(K⁡[t])D\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[t]). Then D′​D​Eα=D′​B=EαD^{\prime}DE_{\alpha}=D^{\prime}B=E_{\alpha}, so D′​D=InD^{\prime}D=I_{n}. It is also readily verified that C⊤​eα=α​eαC^{\top}e_{\alpha}=\alpha e_{\alpha}, where

is the companion matrix of gg. Hence,

D′​A​(D′)−1=(C⊤0⋯00⋱⋱⋮⋮⋱⋱00⋯0C⊤)D^{\prime}A(D^{\prime})^{-1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}C^{\top}&0&\cdots&0\\ 0&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\ 0&\cdots&0&C^{\top}\end{array}\right)

Note that if in all of the above we replace AA by CC (so then m=1m=1), we obtain a proof of the fact that CC is conjugate to C⊤C^{\top}. Combined with the above, this establishes the first statement of this theorem.

Now we turn to the second statement. To explain why we don’t need separability in this case, note that in the proof of the first statement we only used the fact that the rank of KerK⁡(α)⁡(A−α​I)\operatorname{Ker}_{K(\alpha)}(A-\alpha I) is at least mm. So if in the second case we can show directly that the rank is at least 1, we are done by copying the remainder of the proof of the first statement (with m=1m=1).

We will now show that KerK⁡(α)⁡(A−α​I)≠{0}\operatorname{Ker}_{K(\alpha)}(A-\alpha I)\neq\{0\} (which proves that the rank is at least 1). Since g⁡(A)=(A−α​I)​h​(A)g(A)=(A-\alpha I)h(A) for some h​(X)∈K​(α)​[X]h(X)\in K(\alpha)[X], KerK⁡(α)⁡(A−α​I)\operatorname{Ker}_{K(\alpha)}(A-\alpha I) contains the image of h⁡(A)h(A). So it suffices to show that h⁡(A)≠0h(A)\neq 0. To see this, note that h⁡(X)=∑i=0d−1hi​(X)​αih(X)=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}h_{i}(X)\alpha^{i}, where h0,…,hd−1∈K⁡[X]h_{0},\ldots\!,h_{d-1}\in K[X] all have degree strictly less than dd. So hi​(A)≠0h_{i}(A)\neq 0 for all ii, whence h⁡(A)≠0h(A)\neq 0. ∎

Remark 4.16.

In Theorem 4.15 the assumption that the minimal polynomial is irreducible (instead of the more general case of being a power of an irreducible polynomial), is really necessary. Namely, suppose A=In+t​NA=I_{n}+tN, where NN is any nonzero nilpotent matrix in Mn⁡(K)\operatorname{M}_{n}(K). Then (A−In)n=0(A-I_{n})^{n}=0, so the minimal polynomial of AA over K⁡(t)K(t) is a nontrivial power of X−1X-1 (and thus separable). However, AA is not conjugate to an element of GLn⁡(K)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K): for any B∈GLn⁡(K⁡[t])B\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[t]) we have B−1​A​B=I+t​B−1​N​BB^{-1}AB=I+tB^{-1}NB, and t​B−1​N​B∉Mn⁡(K)tB^{-1}NB\notin\operatorname{M}_{n}(K).

Corollary 4.17.

Let KK be a field and A∈GLn⁡(K⁡[t])A\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[t]) satisfying Ad=InA^{d}=I_{n}, where char⁡(K)∤d\operatorname{char}(K)\nmid d. Then there exists a B∈GLn⁡(K⁡[t])B\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[t]) such that B−1​A​B∈GLn⁡(K)B^{-1}AB\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K).

Proof.

Note that the minimal polynomial of AA over K⁡(t)K(t), say g⁡(X)g(X), is an element of K⁡[X]K[X] by Lemma 4.13, and of course a factor of Xd−1X^{d}-1. Since char⁡(K)∤d\operatorname{char}(K)\nmid d, Xd−1X^{d}-1 and its derivative have no common zero in an algebraic closure of KK, so neither do gg and g′g^{\prime}. Hence, gg is a product of mutually coprime monic irreducible polynomials, which are also separable. Using Proposition 4.14, we may reduce to the case that gg is irreducible and separable. But this case is settled by Theorem 4.15. ∎

Theorem 3.7 now gives

Corollary 4.18.

If dd and qq are relatively prime and f∈GAn⁡(𝔽q)(q)f\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{(q)} has finite order dd, then ff is linearizable.

5 Polynomial maps without mixed terms

In this final section we study all problems and conjectures mentioned in the Introduction for the case of a polynomial (map) without mixed terms. KK will be a field, mostly of characteristic zero.

Definition 5.1.

A polynomial f1∈K⁡[X]f_{1}\in K[X] is said to be without mixed terms if we have f1∈K⁡[X1]+⋯+K⁡[Xn]f_{1}\in K[X_{1}]+\cdots+K[X_{n}]. A polynomial map (f1,…,fn)∈K​[X]n(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{n})\in K[X]^{n} (KK a field) is without mixed terms if each of the fif_{i} is.

Linearized polynomial maps are examples of polynomial maps without mixed terms. But the properties of linearized polynomial maps are very different from those of polynomial maps without mixed terms over a zero characteristic field. Namely, we have the following theorem. First, BAn⁡(K)\operatorname{BA}_{n}(K) is the subgroup of triangular automorphisms, i.e. all automorphisms f=(f1,…,fn)f=(f_{1},\ldots\!,f_{n}) with fi−ai​Xi∈K⁡[Xi+1,…,Xn]f_{i}-a_{i}X_{i}\in K[X_{i+1},\ldots\!,X_{n}] and ai∈K∗a_{i}\in K^{*} for all ii. (The notation comes from the fact that BAn⁡(K)∩GLn⁡(K)\operatorname{BA}_{n}(K)\cap\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) equals the Borel subgroup of GLn⁡(K)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K).) Furthermore, such an ff is called unitriangular if a1=⋯=an=1a_{1}=\cdots=a_{n}=1. BAn(1)⁡(K)\operatorname{BA}_{n}^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}(K) will be the subgroup of unitriangular automorphisms.

Theorem 5.2.

Let f∈GAn⁡(K)f\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(K) without mixed terms, and assume further that its linear part equals the identity. If KK has characteristic zero, then there exists a permutation π\pi of the XiX_{i} such that π−1​f​π\pi^{-1}f\pi is unitriangular.

Furthermore, if KK has characteristic p>0p>0, then there exists a permutation π\pi of the XiX_{i} such that π−1fπ∈BAn(1)(K)+(K[X1p]+⋯+K[Xnp])n\pi^{-1}f\pi\in\operatorname{BA}_{n}^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}(K)+(K\big[X_{1}^{{}^{p}}\big]+\cdots+K\big[X_{n}^{{}^{p}}\big])^{{}^{n}}.

Proof.

The first statement is a direct consequence (using Jacobians) of Theorem 5.4, which considers certain matrices with entries in K⁡[X]K[X]. In characteristic p>0p>0 we can use the same theorem, but we need to take into account that the iith partial derivative of a power XimX_{i}^{{}^{m}} vanishes if and only if p|mp\mid m. ∎

Note that, given any automorphism without mixed terms, we can compose it on the left with the inverse of its linear part, to obtain an automorphism satisfying all hypotheses of Theorem 5.2.

Definition 5.3.

A=(ai​j)∈Mn⁡(K⁡[X])A=(a_{ij})\in\operatorname{M}_{n}(K[X]) is a matrix in separated variables if ai​j∈K⁡[Xj]a_{ij}\in K[X_{j}] for all ii and jj. These matrices form a left Mn⁡(K)\operatorname{M}_{n}(K)-submodule of Mn⁡(K⁡[X])\operatorname{M}_{n}(K[X]).

In the following, we use some well-known terminology from matrix theory: A principal submatrix (of order kk) of a square matrix is a submatrix formed by a subset of (kk) rows and the corresponding subset of columns. And a principal (kk-)minor of a square matrix is the determinant of a principal submatrix (of order kk).

Theorem 5.4.

Every matrix A∈GLn⁡(K⁡[X])A\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[X]) in separated variables with A⁡(0)=InA(0)=I_{n} is (after conjugation by a permutation matrix) unitriangular (upper triangular with only 1’s on the diagonal).

Proof.

By Lemma 5.7, we are done if we can prove that all principal minors of AA are equal to 1. First, note that |A|∈K∗|A|\in K^{*} and |A⁡(0)|=1|A(0)|=1 together imply that |A|=1|A|=1. For all 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, let AjA_{j} be the matrix obtained from AA by deleting its jjth row and column. Note that Aj∈Mn−1⁡(K⁡[X^j])A_{j}\in\operatorname{M}_{n-1}(K[\hat{X}_{j}]) is a matrix in seperated variables satisfying Aj​(0)=In−1A_{j}(0)=I_{n-1}. Moreover, expanding the determinant of AA along its jjth column and substituting Xj=0X_{j}=0, we obtain 1=|A|Xj=0|=aj​j(0)⋅|Aj|=|Aj|1=|A_{|_{X_{j}=0}}|=a_{jj}(0)\cdot|A_{j}|=|A_{j}| (A⁡(0)=InA(0)=I_{n}, so ai​j​(0)=0a_{ij}(0)=0 whenever i≠ji\neq j).

From all this we may conclude that for every A∈GLn⁡(K⁡[X])A\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[X]) in separated variables satisfying A⁡(0)=InA(0)=I_{n}, we have |A|=1|A|=1, each AjA_{j} is a matrix in GLn−1⁡(K⁡[X^j])\operatorname{GL}_{n-1}(K[\hat{X}_{j}]) in separated variables and Aj​(0)=In−1A_{j}(0)=I_{n-1}. Induction now proves that for every matrix A∈GLn⁡(K⁡[X])A\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[X]) in separated variables satisfying A⁡(0)=InA(0)=I_{n}, all principal minors are equal to 1. ∎

Remark 5.5.

The proof of the above theorem in particular implies that all diagonal elements of AA (being principal minors) are equal to 1. But this can also be proved directly. Namely, since A⁡(0)=InA(0)=I_{n}, each non-diagonal entry ai​ja_{ij} satisfies Xj|ai​jX_{j}\mid a_{ij}. The fact that A∈GLn⁡(K⁡[X])A\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K[X]) implies that (ai​1​(X1),…,ai​n​(Xn))=(1)(a_{i1}(X_{1}),\ldots\!,a_{in}(X_{n}))=(1) in K⁡[X]K[X] for all ii. Substituting Xj=0X_{j}=0 for all j≠ij\neq i, we obtain ai​i∈K∗a_{ii}\in K^{*}. But A⁡(0)=InA(0)=I_{n}, whence a11=⋯=an​n=1a_{11}=\cdots=a_{nn}=1.

Additionally, Theorem 5.4 partly solves the Jacobian Conjecture:

Corollary 5.6.

The Jacobian Conjecture is satisfied for polynomial maps without mixed terms.

Proof.

If ff is a polynomial map without mixed terms satisfying |J⁡f|∈K∗|\operatorname{J}f|\in K^{*}, then also |J⁡f⁡(0)|∈K∗|\operatorname{J}f(0)|\in K^{*}, i.e. ff has invertible linear part. Composing ff on the left with the inverse of its linear part, we may assume that J⁡f⁡(0)=In\operatorname{J}f(0)=I_{n}. According to Theorem 5.4, this means that ff is unitriangular after a permutation of the variables. ∎

Lemma 5.7.

Let RR be a domain. Suppose A=(ai​j)∈GLn⁡(R)A=(a_{ij})\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(R) has the property that all its principal minors are equal to 1. Then AA is (after conjugation by a permutation matrix) unitriangular.

Proof.

We may assume that RR is a field. Note that if all principal minors of a matrix equal 1, then any principal submatrix also has this property. Further, a column of a square matrix is called an elementary column if its diagonal entry equals 1 and all its remaining entries are 0. Note that the property of having an elementary column is invariant under conjugation by a permutation matrix. (Partly due to the fact that conjugation by a permutation matrix permutes the diagonal elements.)

We will prove the theorem by induction on nn. It is trivial for n=1n=1. If n=2n=2 then |A|=1|A|=1 implies a12​a21=0a_{12}a_{21}=0, which also settles this case (as RR is a field). So we will assume from now on that n≥3n\geq 3 and that the statement holds in lower dimensions. For all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, let AiA_{i} be the matrix obtained from AA by deleting its iith row and column. Note that we may apply the induction hypothesis to AiA_{i}.

We are done if AA contains an elementary column: if this is the case, we may (after permutation) assume that the first column is elementary, and then apply the induction hypothesis to A1A_{1} to obtain (after permutation) a unitriangular matrix.

Now we assume that AA doesn’t have an elementary column, and aim to arrive at a contradiction. Take i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots\!,n\}. By the induction hypothesis, AiA_{i} contains an elementary column. So there is a j≠ij\neq i such that the jjth column of AA is “almost elementary”, i.e. aj​j=1a_{jj}=1 and ak​j=0a_{kj}=0 for k∉{i,j}k\notin\{i,j\}. And ai​j≠0a_{ij}\neq 0, as AA has no elementary column. Associating a jj to each ii in this way, we obtain a map σ\sigma from {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots\!,n\} to itself. σ\sigma is obviously injective, and thus a permutation. Hence, ai​j=0a_{ij}=0 for all ii and jj with j∉{i,σ⁡(i)}j\notin\{i,\sigma(i)\} (and ai​i=1a_{ii}=1 for all ii).

Using the induction hypothesis on AnA_{n} again, we may assume (after conjugation by a permutation matrix) that AnA_{n} is unitriangular. Hence, σ⁡(i)>i\sigma(i)>i for all i<ni<n. But then we must have σ⁡(n)=1\sigma(n)=1 and σ⁡(i)=i+1\sigma(i)=i+1 for all i<ni<n. Hence, expanding the determinant of AA along the nnth row we obtain 0=|A|−1=a1​σ​(1)⋯an​σ​(n)0=|A|-1=a_{1\sigma(1)}\cdots a_{n\sigma(n)}, which contradicts the fact that all ai​σ​(i)a_{i\sigma(i)} are nonzero. ∎

Remark 5.8.

For a domain RR and any A′∈Mn⁡(R)A^{\prime}\in\operatorname{M}_{n}(R), Corollary 6.3.9 in [10] gives a result which is very similar to Lemma 5.7. It says that if every principal minor of A′A^{\prime} is equal to 0, then A′A^{\prime} can be conjugated by a permutation matrix such that the resulting matrix is an upper triangular matrix with zero diagonal. This result and Lemma 5.7 are actually easily shown to be equivalent!

Namely, we can use the well-known fact that the coefficient of Xn−kX^{n-k} in the characteristic polynomial P⋅​(X)P_{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}(X) of an n×nn\times n-matrix equals (−1)k(-1)^{k} times the sum of all principal kk-minors. So suppose A∈GLn⁡(R)A\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(R) is such that all its principal minors are equal to 1. Then any principal submatrix A0′A^{\prime}_{0} of A′:=A−InA^{\prime}:=A-I_{n} is of the form A0′=A0−IA^{\prime}_{0}=A_{0}-I, where II is the identity matrix of the corresponding size, and A0A_{0} is the principal submatrix of AA consisting of the corresponding rows and columns. Let mm be the number of rows (or columns) of A0A_{0}. Since all principal minors of A0A_{0} are equal to 1, and for each kk there are (mk)\binom{m}{k} principal kk-minors, PA0​(X)=Xm−m​Xm−1+(m2)​Xm−2−⋯+(−1)m=(X−1)mP_{A_{0}}(X)=X^{m}-mX^{m-1}+\binom{m}{2}X^{m-2}-\cdots+(-1)^{m}=(X-1)^{m}. But then PA0′​(X)=|X​Im−A0′|=|(X+1)​Im−A0|=PA0​(X+1)=XmP_{A^{\prime}_{0}}(X)=|XI_{m}-A^{\prime}_{0}|=|(X+1)I_{m}-A_{0}|=P_{A_{0}}(X+1)=X^{m}. So A0′A^{\prime}_{0} is nilpotent, and in particular |A0′|=0|A^{\prime}_{0}|=0. Now that every principal minor of A′A^{\prime} is equal to 0, the result in [10] gives a permutation matrix BB such that B−1​A​B=B−1​A′​B+InB^{-1}AB=B^{-1}A^{\prime}B+I_{n} is upper unitriangular. Similarly, we can obtain the result in [10] from our Lemma 5.7.

Now we consider the remaining problems and conjectures presented in the Introduction. First, the Tame Generators Problem: an immediate consequence of Theorem 5.2. (Triangular automorphisms are obviously tame.)

Corollary 5.9.

Over a characteristic zero field, all invertible polynomial maps without mixed terms are tame.

Also, we can use Theorem 5.2 to partly solve the Linearization Conjecture (Corollary 5.11). It is unknown to the author whether this conjecture also holds for the most general form of an invertible polynomial map without mixed terms.

Lemma 5.10.

Let f=(a​X1+p,g)∈GAn⁡(K)f=(aX_{1}+p,g)\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(K), where a∈K∗a\in K^{*}, p∈K⁡[X2,…,Xn]p\in K[X_{2},\ldots\!,X_{n}] and g∈GAn−1⁡(K)g\in\operatorname{GA}_{n-1}(K) (in the variables X2,…,XnX_{2},\ldots\!,X_{n}). Suppose ff has finite order. Then h−1​f​h=(a​X1,g)h^{-1}fh=(aX_{1},g) for some h∈EAn⁡(K)h\in\operatorname{EA}_{n}(K) with h⁡(Xi)=Xih(X_{i})=X_{i} for i≥2i\geq 2.

In particular, the Linearization Conjecture holds for triangular maps.

Proof.

The second statement follows by repeatedly applying the first one to a given triangular map. So let f=(a​X1+p,g)f=(aX_{1}+p,g) be as described, and suppose it has finite order d≥1d\geq 1. One readily verifies that for all k≥1k\geq 1, fkf^{k} has the form (ak​X1+pk,gk)(a^{k}X_{1}+p_{k},g^{k}), where pk∈K⁡[X2,…,Xn]p_{k}\in K[X_{2},\ldots\!,X_{n}] (and pd=0p_{d}=0). From fk+1=fk∘ff^{k+1}=f^{k}\circ f we get that pk+1=pk​(g)+ak​pp_{k+1}=p_{k}(g)+a^{k}p for all kk.

Now let q:=∑k=1d−11d​ak​pkq:=\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\frac{1}{da^{k}}p_{k}, and h:=(X1−q,X2,…,Xn)h:=(X_{1}-q,X_{2},\ldots\!,X_{n}). Then h−1​f​h=(a​X1,g)h^{-1}fh=(aX_{1},g) if and only if −a​q+p+q⁡(g)=0-aq+p+q(g)=0. The latter follows from the fact that q⁡(g)q(g) equals

∑k=1d−11d​ak​pk​(g)=∑k=1d−11d​ak​(pk+1−ak​p)=∑m=2d1d​am−1​pm−d−1d​p=a​q−p\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\tfrac{1}{da^{k}}p_{k}(g)\ =\ \sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\tfrac{1}{da^{k}}(p_{k+1}-a^{k}p)\ =\ \sum_{m=2}^{d}\tfrac{1}{da^{m-1}}p_{m}-\tfrac{d-1}{d}p\ =\ aq-p

using p1=pp_{1}=p and pd=0p_{d}=0. ∎

Corollary 5.11.

Let ff be a polynomial map without mixed terms over a characteristic zero field, and suppose the matrix of its linear part is diagonal. Then the Linearization Conjecture holds for ff.

Proof.

By Theorem 5.2, we may assume that ff is triangular. ∎

The next one (the Coordinate Recognition problem) is easy.

Proposition 5.12.

Let char⁡(K)=0\operatorname{char}(K)=0 and f∈K⁡[X]f\in K[X] a polynomial without mixed terms, say f=f1+⋯+fnf=f_{1}+\cdots+f_{n} with fi∈K⁡[Xi]f_{i}\in K[X_{i}] for all ii. Then ff is a coordinate iff at least one of the fif_{i} has degree 1.

Proof.

A necessary condition for any polynomial in K⁡[X]K[X] to be a coordinate, is that the ideal of its partial derivatives is the unit ideal in K⁡[X]K[X] (as these partial derivatives form the first row of an invertible Jacobian matrix). In this case this condition is also sufficient, since it is here equivalent to saying that at least one of these partial derivatives is a nonzero constant (the partial derivatives cannot have a common zero in an algebraic closure of KK). ∎

Unfortunately, the Polynomial Ring Recognition Problem (say for a finitely generated KK-algebra A=K⁡[X]/IA=K[X]/I, II an ideal) is still unsolved if char⁡(K)=0\operatorname{char}(K)=0 and AA is at least three-generated over KK, even if II is generated by polynomials without mixed terms. In particular, we can finish this paper with the following question.

Question 5.13.

Do polynomials without mixed terms satisfy the Abhyankar-Sathaye Conjecture?

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
